quotes.t: Our society is run by insane people for insane objectives.
We announce the birth of a conceptual country, NUTOPIA. NUTOPIA has no land, no boundaries, no passports, only people.
I've always considered my work one piece and I consider that my work won't be finished until I am dead and buried and I hope that's a long, long time.
We have no more right to consume happiness without producing it than to consume wealth without producing it.
My method is to take the utmost trouble to find the right thing to say, and then to say it with the utmost levity.
There are no secrets better kept than the secrets that everybody guesses.
The gifts of enemies are no gifts and bring no good.
A little word hath often marred, or made, men's fortunes.
Nothing is more hateful than bad counsel.
The historical Jesus will be to our time a stranger and an enigma.
quotes.source: The Quest of the Historical Jesus (1906)

quotes.t: The good conscience is an invention of the devil.
Reverence for life, veneratio vitae, is the most direct and at the same time the profoundest achievement of my will-to-live.
The word impossible is not French.
quotes.source: Letter to General Jean Le Marois, 9 July 1813

quotes.t: A form of government that is not the result of a long sequence of shared experiences, efforts, and endeavors can never take root.
quotes.source: Statement (1803), as quoted in The Mind of Napoleon (1955)

quotes.t: If the art of war were nothing but the art of avoiding risks, glory would become the prey of mediocre minds.... I have made all the calculations; fate will do the rest.
quotes.source: Statement at the beginning of the 1813 campaign, as quoted in The Mind of Napoleon (1955)

quotes.t: Life is a good teacher and a good friend. Things are always in transition, if we could only realize it.
This very moment is the perfect teacher, and, lucky for us, it's with us wherever we are.
Every day, at the moment when things get edgy, we can just ask ourselves, "Am I going to practice peace, or am I going to war?"
A small hole not mended in time will become a big hole much more difficult to mend.
Reading ten thousand books is not as useful as traveling ten thousand miles.
Good medicine tastes bitter.
It would be better for me... that multitudes of men should disagree with me rather than that I, being one, should be out of harmony with myself.
Anyone who holds a true opinion without understanding is like a blind man on the right road.
One should never do wrong in return, nor mistreat any man, no matter how one has been mistreated by him.
Let us not underrate the value of a fact; it will one day flower in a truth.
quotes.source: Natural History of Massachusetts, The Dial (July 1842)

quotes.t: Disobedience is the true foundation of liberty. The obedient must be slaves.

On the death of a friend, we should consider that the fates through confidence have devolved on us the task of a double living, that we have henceforth to fulfill the promise of our friend's life also, in our own, to the world.
It is only due to a lack of heart for the Way and a lack of skill in handling their daily conduct that people become vainly tied to fame and gain.
Zazen is the ultimate practice. This is indeed the True Self. The Buddhadharma is not to be sought outside of this.
Not doing wrong action, sincerely doing every kind of good, naturally clarifies this mind. This is the Teaching of all the Buddhas.
quotes.source: Shoaku makusa (tr. Anzan Hoshin roshi and Yasuda Joshu Dainen roshi, 2007)

quotes.t: The light has gone out of our lives, and there is darkness everywhere. I do not know what to tell you and how to say it.
quotes.source: The Light Has Gone Out (speech, All India Radio, 30 January 1948)

quotes.t: Democracy and socialism are means to an end, not the end itself.

We believe that it is the inalienable right of the Indian people, as of any other people, to have freedom and to enjoy the fruits of their toil and have the necessities of life, so that they may have full opportunities of growth.
Love is born into every human being; it calls back the halves of our original nature together.
Opinion is the medium between knowledge and ignorance.
Time is the moving image of eternity.
Let the punishments of criminals be useful. A hanged man is good for nothing; a man condemned to public works still serves the country, and is a living lesson.
Virtue is debased by self-justification.
In this country it is good to kill an admiral from time to time to encourage the others.
I taste a liquor never brewed, from tankards scooped in pearl.
A narrow fellow in the grass occasionally rides.
I felt a funeral, in my brain, and mourners to and fro kept treading, treading, till it seemed that sense was breaking through.
Please, sir, I want some more.
If the law supposes that, the law is a ass — a idiot.
Annual income twenty pounds, annual expenditure nineteen nineteen six, result happiness. Annual income twenty pounds, annual expenditure twenty pounds ought and six, result misery.
Behold the rain which descends from heaven upon our vineyards; there it enters the roots of the vines, to be changed into wine; a constant proof that God loves us, and loves to see us happy.
In this world nothing can be said to be certain, except death and taxes.
quotes.source: Letter to Jean-Baptiste Le Roy (13 November 1789)

quotes.t: Those who would give up essential Liberty, to purchase a little temporary Safety, deserve neither Liberty nor Safety.
quotes.source: Reply to the Governor, Pennsylvania Assembly (11 November 1755)

quotes.t: A riot is the language of the unheard.
quotes.source: The Other America (speech, Stanford University, 14 April 1967)

quotes.t: We must develop and maintain the capacity to forgive. He who is devoid of the power to forgive is devoid of the power to love.
I have a dream that one day this nation will rise up and live out the true meaning of its creed: 'We hold these truths to be self-evident, that all men are created equal.'
You pierce my soul. I am half agony, half hope.
Silly things do cease to be silly if they are done by sensible people in an impudent way.
The more I know of the world, the more I am convinced that I shall never see a man whom I can really love. I require so much!
Spring is the time of plans and projects.
Rummaging in our souls, we often dig up something that ought to have lain there unnoticed.
There are no conditions to which a man cannot become used, especially if he sees that all around him are living in the same way.
The awful thing is that beauty is mysterious as well as terrible. God and the devil are fighting there and the battlefield is the heart of man.

Love the animals, love the plants, love everything. If you love everything, you will perceive the divine mystery in things. Once you perceive it, you will begin to comprehend it better every day, and you will come at last to love the whole world with an all-embracing love.
The more I love humanity in general, the less I love man in particular.

I see the world gradually being turned into a wilderness, I hear the ever approaching thunder, which will destroy us too, I can feel the sufferings of millions and yet, if I look up into the heavens, I think that it will all come right, that this cruelty too will end, and that peace and tranquility will return again.
quotes.source: The Diary of a Young Girl (entry 15 July 1944)

quotes.t: When the missionaries came to Africa they had the Bible and we had the land. They said 'Let us pray.' We closed our eyes. When we opened them, we had the Bible and they had the land.
Throw your dreams into space like a kite, and you do not know what it will bring back, a new life, a new friend, a new love, a new country.
quotes.source: The Diary of Anais Nin, Vol. IV (1944-1947)

quotes.t: Patience is a remedy for every sorrow.
Wondrous is the strength of cheerfulness, and its power of endurance — the cheerful man will do more in the same time, will do it better, will preserve it longer, than the sad or sullen.
quotes.source: On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History (1841)

quotes.t: The future is dark, which is the best thing the future can be, I think.
A human being in perfection ought always to preserve a calm and peaceful mind, and never to allow passion or a transitory desire to disturb his tranquillity.
If Poetry comes not as naturally as the Leaves to a tree it had better not come at all.
Everything around you that you call life was made up by people that were no smarter than you.
quotes.source: Interview with the Santa Clara Valley Historical Association, 1994

quotes.t: Political democracy cannot last unless there lies at the base of it social democracy.
quotes.source: Speech to the Constituent Assembly, 25 November 1949

quotes.t: In oneself lies the whole world and if you know how to look and learn, the door is there and the key is in your hand. Nobody on earth can give you either the key or the door to open, except yourself.
Never explain — your friends do not need it and your enemies will not believe you anyway.
The man who never looks into a newspaper is better informed than he who reads them.
It is right to learn even from an enemy.
When we can begin to take our failures nonseriously, it means we are ceasing to be afraid of them.
quotes.source: The Journal of Katherine Mansfield (journal entry, October 1922)

quotes.t: I am not an angel, and I will not be one till I die: I will be myself.
I sound my barbaric yawp over the roofs of the world.
quotes.source: Song of Myself, Leaves of Grass

quotes.t: For laws are silent among arms.
Hunger makes a thief of any man.
Life will give you whatever experience is most helpful for the evolution of your consciousness.

I have observed this in my experience of slavery, that whenever my condition was improved, instead of its increasing my contentment, it only increased my desire to be free, and set me to thinking of plans to gain my freedom.
quotes.source: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave (1845)

quotes.t: Love, friendship, respect do not unite people as much as common hatred for something.
People can only live fully by helping others to live. When you give life to friends, you truly live.
quotes.source: The Sun of Jiyu Over a New Land (poem, 1993)

quotes.t: It isn't the mountains ahead to climb that wear you out; it's the pebble in your shoe.
You don't build a business. You build people, and then people build the business.
Faith is what we do with our doubts.
If Algeria introduced a resolution declaring that the earth was flat and that Israel had flattened it, it would pass by a vote of 164 to 13 with 26 abstentions.
There is no power worth defending by bloodshed of the people.
There is virtue in work and there is virtue in rest. Use both and overlook neither.
If I were not Alexander, I would be Diogenes.
The quality of life is more important than life itself.
The greatness of America lies not in being more enlightened than any other nation, but rather in her ability to repair her faults.
It is easier to fight for one's principles than to live up to them.
A map is not the territory it represents, but, if correct, it has a similar structure to the territory, which accounts for its usefulness.
The more things change, the more they stay the same.
You are imperfect, permanently and inevitably flawed. And you are beautiful.

Always bear in mind that the people are not fighting for ideas, for the things in anyone's head. They are fighting to win material benefits, to live better and in peace, to see their lives go forward, to guarantee the future of their children.
Offer your whole-hearted love, let your blood flow to the last drop; if to free her your life is lost, yours is glory then and redemption.
I've learned that the best classroom in the world is at the feet of an elderly person.
Every strike brings me closer to the next home run.
quotes.source: As quoted in Weird Ideas That Work (2001)

A. Powell Davies.bio: British-born American Unitarian clergyman who served as minister of All Souls Church in Washington, D.C. from 1944 until his death. A leading liberal preacher, he was known for defending civil liberties during the McCarthy era.

Abba Eban.bio: Israeli diplomat and Foreign Minister renowned for his oratory at the United Nations.

Abdurrahman Wahid.bio: Abdurrahman Wahid, known as Gus Dur, was an Indonesian Muslim scholar, leader of Nahdlatul Ulama, and Indonesia's fourth president. A defender of pluralism and minorities, he is remembered for the quip that God does not need to be defended.

Alan Cohen.bio: American inspirational author and speaker. His books, including A Deep Breath of Life, focus on spirituality, healing and personal growth.

Albert Schweitzer.bio: Albert Schweitzer was an Alsatian theologian, musician and physician who founded a hospital at Lambaréné in Gabon and served there for decades. His philosophy of reverence for life and his Bach scholarship earned him the Nobel Peace Prize in 1952.

Alexander the Great.bio: King of Macedon who, by the age of thirty, had conquered an empire stretching from Greece to Egypt and northwestern India. He founded more than twenty cities named Alexandria, the most famous in Egypt.

Alexis Carrel.bio: French surgeon and biologist who won the 1912 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his work on vascular suturing and organ transplantation. He later wrote the bestseller Man, the Unknown (1935).

Alexis de Tocqueville.bio: French political thinker and historian most famous for Democracy in America.

Alfred Adler.bio: Austrian physician and psychotherapist who founded the school of individual psychology. He introduced influential concepts including the inferiority complex and the importance of birth order.

Alfred Korzybski.bio: Polish-American scholar who founded general semantics, presented in Science and Sanity (1933). He is famous for the maxim that the map is not the territory.

Alphonse Karr.bio: Jean-Baptiste Alphonse Karr, French critic, journalist and novelist. He coined the famous epigram that the more things change, the more they stay the same.

Amy Bloom.bio: American writer and psychotherapist. She is known for the story collection Come to Me and novels such as Away (2007) and White Houses (2018).

Amílcar Cabral.bio: Amílcar Cabral was an agronomist and revolutionary who led the liberation movement of Guinea-Bissau and Cape Verde against Portuguese colonial rule. He was assassinated in 1973, months before Guinea-Bissau declared independence.

Anais Nin.bio: Anaïs Nin, French-born American diarist and novelist. She is celebrated for her multi-volume Diary, begun when she was eleven, and for works such as Delta of Venus.

Andres Bonifacio.bio: Andres Bonifacio was a Filipino revolutionary who founded the Katipunan, the secret society that launched the Philippine Revolution against Spain in 1896. A warehouse clerk by trade, he was also a poet of fierce love for his homeland.

Andy Rooney.bio: American radio and television writer best known for A Few Minutes with Andy Rooney, his closing segment on CBS's 60 Minutes from 1978 to 2011. His humorous essays on everyday life made him a household voice.

Anne Frank.bio: German-born Jewish diarist whose diary documents life in hiding during the Holocaust.

Anton Chekhov.bio: Anton Chekhov was a Russian playwright and master of the short story, a practising doctor who wrote The Cherry Orchard, Uncle Vanya and hundreds of stories. His restrained, humane art reshaped both the theatre and short fiction of the 20th century.

B.R. Ambedkar.bio: Indian jurist and social reformer who chaired the drafting of India's Constitution and campaigned against caste discrimination.

Babe Ruth.bio: George Herman 'Babe' Ruth, American baseball legend. His prodigious home-run hitting with the New York Yankees, 714 in his career, transformed baseball and made him a national icon.

Benjamin Franklin.bio: American polymath - printer, scientist, diplomat - and a Founding Father of the United States.

Charles Dickens.bio: English novelist and social critic; author of A Christmas Carol, Oliver Twist and Great Expectations.

Charlotte Brontë.bio: English novelist, author of Jane Eyre.
Charlotte Brontë.credit: Alonzo Chappel, Public domain (File: File:Charlotte Bronte by Alonzo Chappel.jpg)

Cicero.bio: Marcus Tullius Cicero was a Roman statesman, lawyer and orator considered the master of Latin prose. His speeches, letters and philosophical works, including On Friendship, transmitted Greek philosophy to the Roman world.

Daisaku Ikeda.bio: Daisaku Ikeda was a Japanese Buddhist philosopher, educator and peace activist who led the Soka Gakkai lay Buddhist movement and founded Soka University. He wrote extensively on Buddhism, dialogue and peace.

Desmond Tutu.bio: South African Anglican archbishop and Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1984) who campaigned against apartheid.

Dogen.bio: Founder of the Sōtō school of Zen in Japan and author of the Shōbōgenzō, a landmark of Buddhist philosophy.

Eckhart Tolle.bio: Eckhart Tolle is a German-born spiritual teacher living in Canada, author of The Power of Now (1997) and A New Earth (2005), books on presence and the ego that became international bestsellers.

Elbert Hubbard.bio: Elbert Hubbard was an American writer, publisher and philosopher who founded the Roycroft arts-and-crafts community. His essay "A Message to Garcia" (1899) was one of the most widely reprinted works of its era; he died in the sinking of the Lusitania.

Emily Dickinson.bio: American poet whose nearly 1,800 poems, mostly unpublished in her lifetime, made her a central figure of American literature.
Emily Dickinson.credit: Miscellaneous Items in High Demand, PPOC, Library of Congress, Public domain

Frederick Douglass.bio: American abolitionist and writer who escaped slavery and became a leading voice against it.

Fyodor Dostoevsky.bio: Russian novelist, author of Crime and Punishment and The Brothers Karamazov.

George Bernard Shaw.bio: Irish playwright and critic; author of Pygmalion; Nobel Prize in Literature 1925.
George Bernard Shaw.credit: Sussman, Public domain (File: George Bernard Shaw, playwright (SAYRE 9001).jpg)

Henry David Thoreau.bio: American writer known for Walden (1854) and the essay Civil Disobedience.

Jane Austen.bio: English novelist known for Pride and Prejudice and Emma, celebrated for irony and social observation.
Jane Austen.credit: Engraving by William Home Lizars after James Andrews, Public domain

Jawaharlal Nehru.bio: Leader of India's independence movement and the country's first Prime Minister (1947-1964).

Jiddu Krishnamurti.bio: Indian philosopher and speaker on the nature of mind, meditation, and human freedom; rejected all guru roles.

John Keats.bio: English Romantic poet of the great Odes, including Ode to a Nightingale.

John Lennon.bio: English singer-songwriter, co-founder of the Beatles and solo artist known for Imagine.

Katherine Mansfield.bio: New Zealand modernist short-story writer, a leading figure of early 20th-century literature alongside Joyce and Woolf.
Katherine Mansfield.credit: Archives New Zealand from New Zealand, CC BY-SA 2.0

Leo Tolstoy.bio: Russian novelist, author of War and Peace and Anna Karenina.

Martin Luther King Jr..bio: American Baptist minister who led the civil rights movement; Nobel Peace Prize laureate 1964.

Mary Shelley.bio: English novelist, author of Frankenstein, a founding work of science fiction.

Muhammad Ali.bio: American heavyweight boxing champion and cultural icon known as much for his activism as his titles.

Napoleon Bonaparte.bio: Napoleon Bonaparte was a French military leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution and became Emperor of the French in 1804. His Napoleonic Wars reshaped Europe, and his Napoleonic Code influenced legal systems worldwide. He died in exile on Saint Helena.

Ovid.bio: Ovid was a Roman poet celebrated for the Metamorphoses, a vast narrative poem of mythological transformations. Exiled by the emperor Augustus to the Black Sea coast, he spent his last decade writing poems of lament and endurance.

Pearl Buck.bio: Pearl S. Buck was an American writer who spent much of her early life in China, where her parents were missionaries. Her novel The Good Earth won the Pulitzer Prize, and she received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1938.

Pema Chodron.bio: Pema Chodron is an American nun in the Tibetan Buddhist tradition and a widely read author and teacher. Her books, including When Things Fall Apart, bring Buddhist teachings on compassion and difficulty to a broad audience.

Plato.bio: Greek philosopher, student of Socrates and author of The Republic.

Publilius Syrus.bio: Publilius Syrus was a Latin writer of the 1st century BC who was brought to Italy as a slave from Syria and later freed. He is known for his Sententiae, a collection of moral maxims drawn from his mimes.

Socrates.bio: Greek philosopher of Athens, central figure of Western philosophy; left no writings.

Sophocles.bio: Sophocles was an Athenian tragedian who wrote more than 120 plays, of which seven survive complete. Oedipus Rex and Antigone, his most famous works, set the pattern for Western tragedy.

Steve Jobs.bio: Co-founder of Apple, Steve Jobs helped launch the personal computer era and later reinvented music, phones and tablets with the iPod, iPhone and iPad. Forced out of Apple in 1985, he founded NeXT and built Pixar into a major studio before returning in 1997 to rescue the company he had started.

Thomas Carlyle.bio: Thomas Carlyle was a Scottish historian, philosopher and essayist whose works, including Sartor Resartus and On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History, shaped Victorian thought. His history of the French Revolution is regarded as a classic of the genre.

Thomas Jefferson.bio: Thomas Jefferson was an American statesman and Founding Father who wrote the Declaration of Independence and served as the third President of the United States (1801–1809). He founded the University of Virginia and doubled the nation's size with the Louisiana Purchase.

Virginia Woolf.bio: Virginia Woolf was an English writer and a central figure of literary modernism, famous for stream-of-consciousness novels such as Mrs Dalloway (1925) and To the Lighthouse (1927). Her essay A Room of One's Own (1929) became a foundational feminist text on women and writing. With her husband Leonard she founded the Hogarth Press, which published her own work and that of T. S. Eliot and others.

Voltaire.bio: Voltaire, born François-Marie Arouet, was a French Enlightenment writer, philosopher and historian famous for the novella Candide and for his witty defence of civil liberties, including freedom of speech and religion. He was one of the most prolific and influential writers of his age.

Walt Whitman.bio: American poet best known for the collection Leaves of Grass (1855).

Zig Ziglar.bio: Zig Ziglar was an American author and motivational speaker who became one of the most influential sales and personal-development trainers of the twentieth century. His book See You at the Top and his famous line 'Your attitude, not your aptitude, will determine your altitude' reached millions.
